about: A rewrite of the Linux user account tools (useradd, usermod, passwd and others) in Rust, aiming to work the same as GNU shadow.

prs.title: useradd now gives the right exit code for a bad user name
prs.broken: useradd exited with code 3 when a user name was not allowed. The manual says it should exit with 19, and GNU useradd does.
prs.changed: A rejected user name now exits with 19, and other errors keep their codes.
prs.matters: Scripts that check why useradd failed get the answer the manual promises.

prs.title: useradd and usermod now accept -1 to clear expiry settings
prs.broken: The manuals say -1 clears the account expiry date and the inactive days, but both tools rejected -1 as an unknown option.
prs.changed: The expiry and inactive options now take -1 and clear the field, as in GNU shadow.
prs.matters: Commands and scripts written for GNU shadow work here unchanged.

prs.title: useradd -U always creates the user's group
prs.broken: When the system setting for user groups was off, useradd -U quietly skipped creating the user's own group. It also accepted -U together with -g.
prs.changed: -U now always creates the group, and -U with -g is rejected, as in GNU shadow.
prs.matters: Scripts that ask for a user group get one, whatever the system default is.

prs.title: Changing a user's group also updates their home files
prs.broken: Changing a user's primary group left the files in their home directory in the old group, unlike GNU usermod.
prs.changed: The home directory walk now moves files from the old group to the new one, changes links rather than their targets, and skips homes the user does not own.
prs.matters: After a group change, the user's files belong to their new group, as admins expect.

prs.title: System accounts now get IDs from the top of the range
prs.broken: useradd -r and groupadd -r gave a new system account the lowest free ID, for example 101. GNU shadow starts at the top of the range and counts down.
prs.changed: System users and groups now get the highest free system ID, 999 on a fresh system, then 998, the same as GNU.
prs.matters: Machines set up with these tools hand out the same system IDs as other Linux systems.

prs.title: chage can now print dates as YYYY-MM-DD
prs.broken: chage did not accept -i or --iso8601, so there was no way to get the password aging dates in a fixed year-month-day form.
prs.changed: chage -l -i now prints every aging date as YYYY-MM-DD, matching GNU chage. Without -i the output stays the same.
prs.matters: Scripts can read password expiry dates without parsing month names.

prs.title: passwd now says "password changed." like GNU passwd
prs.broken: After locking, unlocking or changing the aging of an account, passwd printed its own message on the error stream, unlike GNU passwd.
prs.changed: It now prints "passwd: password changed." on normal output, the same line GNU passwd prints. With -q it stays silent.
prs.matters: Scripts and logs that expect GNU's message see it, and a success no longer looks like an error.

prs.title: chfn and chsh stay quiet after a successful change
prs.broken: chfn and chsh printed a line on the error stream after every successful change. GNU chfn and chsh print nothing.
prs.changed: The extra line is gone. Errors and the interactive prompts work as before.
prs.matters: Scripts that treat any error output as a failure no longer flag a change that worked.

prs.title: usermod can move a home folder
prs.broken: The Rust usermod had no -m option, so changing a user's home path left their files behind.
prs.changed: usermod -m now moves the old home to the new path, copying across disks with owners, modes and times kept.
prs.matters: Admins can rename or relocate a user's home in one step, as with the original tool.

prs.title: pwck stays quiet when the files are fine
prs.broken: pwck warned about the normal nobody account on every Debian or Ubuntu system, and said no changes even when nothing was wrong.
prs.changed: The false warning is gone, and no changes now appears only after real problems, as in the original.
prs.matters: A clean system gives a clean check.

prs.title: Changing group members updates both group files
prs.broken: groupmod -U changed the members in one group file but not in the shadow group file, so the two disagreed.
prs.changed: The same member change now goes to both files.
prs.matters: Group membership stays consistent everywhere the system looks for it.

prs.title: usermod can take a user out of some groups
prs.broken: usermod had no -r option, so removing a user from a few groups meant listing every group they should stay in.
prs.changed: usermod -r -G now removes the user from just the groups named and keeps the rest.
prs.matters: Admins can drop a group membership without touching the others.

prs.title: Group and user IDs can no longer be set to a reserved value
prs.broken: groupadd and usermod accepted 4294967295 as an ID, a value the system treats as meaning no change.
prs.changed: Both now refuse it, as the other commands and the original tools already do.
prs.matters: Accounts can't end up with an ID that file permissions quietly ignore.
